                                   4                                   UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT

                                   7     MICHAEL GARCIA, et al.,                            Case No. 25-cv-11078-JSC
                                                        Plaintiffs,

                                                                                            ORDER TO PLAINTIFFS TO SHOW
                                                 v.                                         CAUSE RE: ARTICLE III STANDING
                                   9

                                  10     MICROSOFT CORPORATION, et al.,                     Re: Dkt. No. 20
                                                        Defendants.
                                  11

                                  12
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13           Plaintiffs filed in federal court this putative class action against Microsoft Corporation and

                                  14   Mojang AB on behalf of California residents who used Defendants’ Minecraft websites,

                                  15   applications, and related online services, from within the State of California. (Dkt. No. 20 at ¶ 1.)

                                  16   They allege Defendants instrumented Minecraft-branded properties “with tracking technologies—

                                  17   including session replay, keystroke and mouse-movement logging, device fingerprinting,

                                  18   telemetry collection, and embedded analytics and video integrations—that intercept, record, and

                                  19   transmit the contents of users’ communications and detailed behavioral data in real time” (id. ¶ 2),

                                  20   in violation of various California laws. In connection with the pending motion to compel

                                  21   arbitration the Court reviewed the Amended Complaint. As that review raises concerns about the

                                  22   Court’s subject matter jurisdiction, Plaintiffs are ORDERED TO SHOW CAUSE as to whether

                                  23   the Court has Article III standing over each Plaintiff’s claims.

                                  24          Federal courts are courts of “limited jurisdiction” which “possess only that power

                                  25   authorized by Constitution and statute.” Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Ins. Co. of Am., 511 U.S. 375,

                                  26   377 (1994). Article III of the United States Constitution “confines the federal judicial power to the

                                  27   resolution of ‘Cases’ and ‘Controversies.’” TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413, 423

                                  28   (2021). “For there to be a case or controversy under Article III, the plaintiff must have a ‘personal
                                         Case 3:25-cv-11078-JSC           Document 45          Filed 09/25/26     Page 2 of 4




                                   1   stake’ in the case—in other words, standing.” Id. (citations omitted). Article III standing can be

                                   2   raised any time including sua sponte by the court. City of Los Angeles v. Cnty. of Kern, 581 F.3d

                                   3   841, 845 (9th Cir. 2009). Indeed, federal courts have an “obligation to be sure that standing exists

                                   4   and to raise, sua sponte if need be, any deficiency.” San Francisco Drydock, Inc. v. Dalton, 131

                                   5   F.3d 776, 778 (9th Cir. 1997).

                                   6          To establish standing sufficient to satisfy constitutional requirements, “a plaintiff must

                                   7   show (i) that he suffered an injury in fact that is concrete, particularized, and actual or imminent;

                                   8   (ii) that the injury was likely caused by the defendant; and (iii) that the injury would likely be

                                   9   redressed by judicial relief.” Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555, 560–561 (1992)). In a

                                  10   putative class action, at least one named plaintiff must have Article III standing. See Healy v.

                                  11   Milliman, Inc., 164 F.4th 701, 706 (9th Cir. 2026). Plaintiffs, as the parties invoking federal

                                  12   jurisdiction, bear the burden of establishing standing. See Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins, 578 U.S. 330,
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   338 (2016).

                                  14          A “concrete” injury can include “intangible harms,” such as “reputational harms,

                                  15   disclosure of private information, and intrusion upon seclusion.” TransUnion, 594 U.S. at 425. In

                                  16   Popa, the Ninth Circuit addressed Article III standing in privacy cases such as this. Popa v.

                                  17   Microsoft Corp., 153 F.4th 784 (9th Cir. 2025) There, the plaintiff alleged the defendant’s session-

                                  18   replay technology captured her information while she browsed for pet supplies on a pet supply

                                  19   website. In particular, “[t]he information [the] defendant collected allegedly included: the date the

                                  20   user visited the website, the device the user accessed the website on, the type of browser the user

                                  21   accessed the website on, the operating system of the device used to access the website, the country

                                  22   where the user accessed the website from, a user’s mouse movements, a user’s screen swipes, text

                                  23   inputted by the user on the website, and how far down a webpage a user scrolls, the user’s mailing

                                  24   address with the street number and zip code omitted, and the pet supplies products the user clicked

                                  25   on.” Krzyzek v. OpenX Techs., Inc., 817 F. Supp. 3d 857, 863 (N.D. Cal. 2026) (citing Popa, 153

                                  26   F.4th at 786-87, 791). The Ninth Circuit affirmed the district court’s dismissal for lack of Article

                                  27   III standing because the nature of the collected information was not “embarrassing, invasive, or

                                  28   otherwise private.” Id. at 786-87, 791. The court held the plaintiff had not established “how the
                                                                                          2
                                         Case 3:25-cv-11078-JSC            Document 45          Filed 09/25/26      Page 3 of 4




                                   1   tracking of her interactions ... caused her to experience any kind of harm that is remotely similar to

                                   2   the ‘highly offensive’ interferences or disclosures that were actionable at common law.” Id. at 791.

                                   3   The court explained further “the kind of harm and not the degree” is relevant for determining

                                   4   whether an alleged injury-in-fact is concrete enough relative “to a specific common-law tort” and

                                   5   that the injury must be one “that has traditionally been actionable in our nation’s legal system.” Id.

                                   6           The Amended Complaint includes a specific section purporting to allege standing. (Dkt.

                                   7   No. 20 at ¶¶ 50-53.) However, the allegations do not include any facts that support a plausible

                                   8   inference the tracking of each Plaintiff’s interactions with Minecraft caused the plaintiff “to

                                   9   experience any kind of harm that is remotely similar to the ‘highly offensive’ interferences or

                                  10   disclosures that were actionable at common law” because the allegations are wholly generic. For

                                  11   example, the Amended Complaint alleges Plaintiff Gavin Hays “used the Minecraft Properties for

                                  12   consumer purposes, including through his own account, and his communications, browsing
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   activity, interaction data, device data, and persistent identifiers were intercepted, and transmitted

                                  14   by Defendants’ tracking technologies without valid consent.” (Id. ¶ 50.) Similarly, the Amended

                                  15   Complaint alleges Plaintiff Dart’s “own communications, personal information, payment-related

                                  16   information, device data, and persistent identifiers were intercepted.” (Id. ¶ 51.) The minor

                                  17   plaintiffs similarly allege tracking of non-specific data and no effort is made to identify the

                                  18   disclosure of data that were actionable at common law. (Id. ¶¶ 52, 53.) These generic, non-

                                  19   specific allegations do not appear to satisfy the showing required for Article III standing.

                                  20           So, the Court is concerned it lacks subject matter jurisdiction. Accordingly, on or before

                                  21   October 16, 2026, Plaintiffs shall show cause in writing as to the Court’s subject matter

                                  22   jurisdiction over this action. A determination Plaintiffs lack Article III standing is not a ruling on

                                  23   the merits; instead, if the Court rule it lacks subject matter jurisdiction it will dismiss the action

                                  24   without prejudice to Plaintiffs pursuing their claims in California state court. See, e.g., Nat'l Coal.

                                  25   for Men v. Selective Serv. Sys., No. 24-7746, 2025 WL 3485392, at *1 (9th Cir. Dec. 4, 2025),

                                  26   cert. denied, 146 S. Ct. 2717 (2026) (“Because Plaintiffs lack Article III standing, we vacate the

                                  27   district court’s grant of the 12(b)(6) motion and remand with instructions to dismiss this case

                                  28   without prejudice”).
                                                                                           3

                                   2   rescheduled when, and if, the Court determines it has subject matter jurisdiction.

                                   3          IT IS SO ORDERED.

                                   4   Dated: September 25, 2026

 1          Plaintiffs’ administrative motion should be denied for three independent reasons.

 2          First, the supplemental declarations are procedurally improper. Under this District’s local

 3   rules, “[o]nce a reply is filed, no additional memoranda, papers or letters may be filed without

 4   prior Court approval.” Civil L.R. 7-3(d). The Court’s June 8 order instructed that “Defendants

 5   shall provide Plaintiffs with a supplemental declaration,” but it said nothing about Plaintiffs

 6   providing additional evidence. Dkt. 33 at 3.

 7          Second, even if the Court’s June 8 order did provide a basis for Plaintiffs to submit new

 8   evidence, Plaintiffs’ supplemental declarations are untimely. The June 8 order directed the parties

 9   to meet and confer after Defendants had provided Plaintiffs with Defendants’ supplemental
10   declarations and then “file a joint submission by June 26, that sets forth their agreements and
11   disagreements.” Dkt. 33 at 3. In light of that instruction, Plaintiffs should have—at a minimum—
12   shared any new proposed evidence with Defendants before the parties’ June 22 meet and confer
13   and then attached it to the parties’ June 26 joint submission. That is precisely what Defendants
14   did: They served their supplemental declarations on Plaintiffs on June 15 and attached them to the
15   parties’ joint submission. Plaintiffs, however, did not share their supplemental declarations with
16   Defendants until July 1.
17          Third, in any event, the supplemental declarations fail to create a genuine factual dispute
18   about whether Gavin Hays and Alyce Itsuye Dart entered enforceable agreements to arbitrate under
19   the Microsoft Services Agreement (“MSA”). Indeed, Ms. Dart’s declaration does not appear to be
20   new or “supplemental” at all: It is word-for-word identical to a declaration she previously
21   submitted (including with respect to the May 26 execution date). Compare Dkt. 31-1, with Dkt.
22   37-3. And it relates to Defendants’ arguments regarding Ms. Dart’s purported disaffirmance on
23   A.D.’s behalf, not contract formation. As for Mr. Hays’s declaration, it primarily consists of claims
24   that he does not recall certain things. See Dkt. 37-2 ¶¶ 5, 8-11. As Defendants (Reply 4-5) and
25   this Court (Dkt. 33 at 5) have already explained, a plaintiff’s inability to remember aspects of the
26   account-creation process does not defeat evidence of reasonable notice. In addition, Mr. Hays’s
27   assertion of what the account-creation process “caused [him] to understand” (Dkt. 37-2 ¶ 13) is
28

 1   immaterial because contract interpretation is based on “objective intent, as evidenced by the words

 2   of the contract, rather than the subjective intent of one of the parties.” Bodenburg v. Apple Inc.,

 3   146 F.4th 761, 767 (9th Cir. 2025); see also Reply 5; Dkt. 36 at 6. Mr. Hays’s new declaration

 4   now (for the first time) attempts to fault the Microsoft account-creation process because the

 5   hyperlink to the MSA did not itself expressly mention the arbitration provision (see Dkt. 37-2

 6   ¶ 12); this argument is foreclosed by the Ninth Circuit and California precedent cited in

 7   Defendants’ papers, which have enforced contracts even where the hyperlinked text did not

 8   explicitly mention the relevant contracts’ arbitration provisions. See, e.g., Keebaugh v. Warner

 9   Bros. Ent. Inc., 100 F.4th 1005, 1011 (9th Cir. 2024) (cited by MTC 8-10, 11, 15; Reply 2-3, 12).
10          For these reasons, Plaintiffs’ administrative motion should be denied.

 8   purposes of analyzing reasonably conspicuous notice of contractual terms, a declaration containing

 9   a screenshot substantially similar to what a plaintiff saw at the time of assent is adequate to
10   establish how the screen appeared. See Reply 3-4 (discussing cases). Evidence of exactly how a
11   screen appeared to a particular plaintiff at the exact moment that the plaintiff signed up is not
12   required. See id.; Hong v. StubHub, Inc., 2024 WL 4720924, at *3-4 (C.D. Cal. Sept. 9, 2024)
13   (cited by Dkt. 33 at 5) (granting motion to compel based on “purchase process as it would have

19   First Scari Decl. ¶ 10) or historical moment-in-time screenshots to establish contract formation.

22   of content from the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine,” J.J. v. Ashlynn Mktg. Grp., Inc., 2026

25   11436309, at *4 (N.D. Cal. Oct. 3, 2018) (Corley, J.) (alteration adopted) (quoting Fed. R. Evid.

28   of “the Wayback Machine link in the footnote of Defendants’ motion”); Brown v. Madison Reed,

20   Cal. Apr. 10, 2026). Defendants’ “unrebutted evidence that the screenshot[s are] substantially
21   similar to what [Mr. Hays and Ms. Dart] would have seen” at the relevant times, as well as account-
22   specific data reflecting the exact date and time of account creation, more than “satisfies
23   [Defendants’] burden” to establish contract formation. Hong, 2024 WL 4720924, at *4. A
24   “[p]laintiff’s mere assertion that a factual dispute exists is insufficient to require discovery,” but
25   that is all Mr. Hays and Ms. Dart offer. Voll, 2019 WL 144863, at *4; accord Tomlin v. Roblox
26   Corp., 2026 WL 1412606, at *10 (E.D. Pa. May 20, 2026) (cited by Dkt. 32) (“Mere speculation”
27   that Microsoft sign-up process might have proceeded unusually did “not create a genuine dispute

 1          Mr. Hays’s and Ms. Dart’s anticipated supplemental declarations, as described by their

 2   counsel to Defendants’ counsel, are both legally irrelevant and procedurally improper. It does not

 3   matter whether Mr. Hays and Ms. Dart would not have created their accounts had they seen the

 4   arbitration agreement or the class-action waiver in the MSA. As Defendants have explained (MTC

 5   12; Reply 5), “parties to a contract are generally deemed to have consented to all the terms of a

 6   contract they sign, even if they have not read it.” Chamber of Com. of the U.S. v. Bonta, 62 F.4th

 7   473, 488 (9th Cir. 2023). Contract interpretation is based on “the objective intent, as evidenced by

 8   the words of the contract, rather than the subjective intent of one of the parties.” Bodenburg v.

 9   Apple Inc., 146 F.4th 761, 767 (9th Cir. 2025). Here, Mr. Hays and Ms. Dart agreed to the MSA
10   because, as Defendants’ supplemental declarations conclusively establish, they had “reasonably
11   conspicuous notice” of the MSA and clicked buttons that “unambiguously manifest[ed their]
12   assent” to the MSA. Patrick v. Running Warehouse, LLC, 93 F.4th 468, 476 (9th Cir. 2024). Thus,
13   whether Mr. Hays and Ms. Dart had “actual knowledge of the [MSA]” is beside the point. Id. The
14   best, and only proper, evidence of what Mr. Hays and Ms. Dart intended in agreeing to the MSA
15   is its text. That text clearly states, in conspicuous font, that the MSA has a “BINDING
16   ARBITRATION CLAUSE AND CLASS ACTION WAIVER IN SECTION 15.” First Scari
17   Decl., Ex. A at 1; see id. § 15; MTC 3-4. And, in any event, Plaintiffs’ declarations are procedurally
18   improper. “Once a reply is filed, no additional memoranda, papers or letters may be filed without
19   prior Court approval,” with two inapplicable exceptions. Civil L.R. 7-3(d); see Del Campo v. Am.
20   Corrective Counseling Servs., Inc., 718 F. Supp. 2d 1116, 1121 n.4 (N.D. Cal. 2010) (striking post-
21   briefing filing as “an improper attempt to file a surreply brief without leave of the Court”). The
22   Court ordered Defendants to submit a supplemental declaration, but the Court did not permit (let
23   alone direct) Plaintiffs to do so. See generally Dkt. 33.
24          In sum, Defendants’ supplemental declarations establish that Mr. Hays and Ms. Dart agreed
25   to the MSA, which contains an arbitration provision compelling arbitration of their and A.D.’s
26   claims. Therefore, the Court should deny Plaintiffs’ request for discovery and grant Defendants’
27   motion to compel arbitration of Mr. Hays’s, Ms. Dart’s, and A.D.’s claims and stay R.G.’s claims
28   pending arbitration of the other Plaintiffs’ claims. If the Court is inclined to order any discovery,

                                  14            Plaintiffs filed this putative class action bringing privacy claims against Microsoft and

                                  15   Mojang AB alleging Defendants secretly tracked the contents of their communications when using

                                  16   Defendants’ Minecraft-branded technologies. Defendants have moved to compel arbitration as to

                                  17   three Plaintiffs: Gavin Hays, Alyce Itsuye Dart, and Ms. Dart’s minor child A.D, based on an

                                  18   arbitration agreement in the Microsoft Services Agreement, which Defendants contend all users

                                  19   must accept as part of the account creation process.1 (Dkt. No. 24.2) The parties’ briefing

                                  20   indicates there is a dispute as to contract formation. The Court thus VACATES the June 18, 2026

                                  21   hearing on the motion to compel arbitration and orders the parties to meet and confer as set forth

                                  22   below.

                                  23                                               DISCUSSION

                                  24            The Federal Arbitration Act (“FAA”) provides arbitration agreements “shall be valid,

                                  25   irrevocable, and enforceable, save upon such grounds as exist at law or in equity for revocation of

                                  26
                                       1
                                  27       Defendants move to stay Plaintiff R.G.’s claims pending arbitration.
                                       2
                                  28    Record citations are to material in the Electronic Case File (“ECF”); pinpoint citations are to the
                                       ECF-generated page numbers at the top of the documents.
                                            Case 3:25-cv-11078-JSC        Document 33        Filed 06/08/26      Page 2 of 6




                                   1   any contract.” 9 U.S.C. § 2. Under the FAA, “arbitration agreements [are] on an equal footing with

                                   2   other contracts,” and therefore courts must “enforce them according to their terms.” Rent-A-

                                   3   Center, West, Inc. v. Jackson, 561 U.S. 63, 67 (2010) (internal citations omitted). A party may

                                   4   petition a court to compel “arbitration [to] proceed in the manner provided for in such agreement.”

                                   5   9 U.S.C. § 4. A court must compel arbitration should it determine: (1) a valid arbitration

                                   6   agreement exists; and (2) “the agreement encompasses the dispute at issue.” Berman v. Freedom

                                   7   Fin. Network, LLC, 30 F.4th 849, 855 (9th Cir. 2022) (internal citation omitted). Defendants, as

                                   8   the parties moving to compel arbitration, bear the burden of establishing the existence of valid

                                   9   arbitration agreements. See Knutson v. Sirius XM Radio Inc., 771 F.3d 559, 565 (9th Cir. 2014).

                                  10   Plaintiffs Gavin Hays and Alyce Dart oppose arbitration arguing, in part, Defendants have not

                                  11   demonstrated the existence of a valid agreement to arbitrate.3

                                  12           The existence of an arbitration agreement is a question for the Court, not an arbitrator. See
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   Knutson v. Sirius XM Radio Inc., 771 F.3d 559, 565 (9th Cir. 2014); see also Reichert v. Rapid

                                  14   Invs., Inc., 826 F. App’x 656, 658 (9th Cir. 2020) (“Notwithstanding any delegation clause in the

                                  15   Agreement, ‘challenges to the existence of a contract as a whole must be determined by the court

                                  16   prior to ordering arbitration.’”) (cleaned up). When, as here, “the making of the arbitration

                                  17   agreement” is at issue, the summary judgment standard applies. Hansen v. LMB Mortg. Servs.,

                                  18   Inc., 1 F.4th 667, 670 (9th Cir. 2021) (quoting 9 U.S.C. § 4). To prevail under the summary

                                  19   judgment standard, Defendants must show there is no genuine issue as to any material fact

                                  20   regarding formation of the arbitration contract. Id.; see also Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S.

                                  21   317, 322 (1986).

                                  22           “In determining whether the parties have agreed to arbitrate a particular dispute, federal

                                  23   courts apply state-law principles of contract formation.” Berman v. Freedom Fin. Network, LLC,

                                  24   30 F.4th 849, 855 (9th Cir. 2022). “To form a contract under ... California law, the parties must

                                  25   manifest their mutual assent to the terms of the agreement.” Id. “Parties traditionally manifest

                                  26
                                  27   3
                                         Defendants insist Ms. Dart assented to arbitration on A.D.’s behalf. Thus, the arbitrability of her
                                  28   claims is dependent, at least in part, on whether there is a valid arbitration agreement with Ms.
                                       Dart.
                                                                                          2
                                         Case 3:25-cv-11078-JSC           Document 33         Filed 06/08/26     Page 3 of 6




                                   1   assent by written or spoken word, but they can also do so through conduct.” Id. “However, ‘[t]he

                                   2   conduct of a party is not effective as a manifestation of his assent unless he intends to engage in

                                   3   the conduct and knows or has reason to know that the other party may infer from his conduct that

                                   4   he assents.’” Id. (alteration in original) (quoting Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 19(2)

                                   5   (1981)). “These elemental principles of contract formation apply with equal force to contracts

                                   6   formed online. Thus, if a website offers contractual terms to those who use the site, and a user

                                   7   engages in conduct that manifests her acceptance of those terms, an enforceable agreement can be

                                   8   formed.” Id. at 855–56.

                                   9          To avoid the unfairness of enforcing contractual terms that consumers never intended to

                                  10   accept, courts considering online agreements “have devised rules to determine whether meaningful

                                  11   assent has been given.” Id. at 856. Unless the website operator can demonstrate actual knowledge

                                  12   of the agreement, an enforceable contract will be found based on an inquiry notice theory only if:
